question.problem: A pastry shop is famous for its chocolate cakes. On average, only $20%$ of the shop's customers prefer to buy a type of cake other than chocolate. What is the probability that the first customer who decides not to buy a chocolate cake appears before the $4$th customer?
question.worked_solution:
A geometric random variable $X$ with probability of success $p$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(1-p)^{x-1}p
$$

Let $X$ be the number of customers served until one customer decides not to buy a chocolate cake. Since the chance of a single customer deciding not to buy a chocolate cake is $20%,$ the number of customers served until one decides against chocolate cake can be modeled as a geometric random variable with a probability of success

$$
p=20%=\frac{20}{100}=0.2.
$$

So, $X∼\text{Geom}(0.2).$ In this case, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(1-0.2)^{x-1}(0.2) \\  & =(0.8)^{x-1}(0.2)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability the first customer who decides not to buy a chocolate cake appears before the $4$th customer is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<4) & =P(X\in \{1,2,3\}) \\  & =f(1)+f(2)+f(3) \\  & =(0.8)^{1-1}(0.2)+(0.8)^{2-1}(0.2)+(0.8)^{3-1}(0.2) \\  & =(0.2)+(0.8)(0.2)+(0.8)^{2}(0.2) \\  & =[1+0.8+(0.8)^{2}](0.2) \\  & =0.488.\end{aligned}
$$
